summary: A response to RFC 328 objecting to two of its three proposed Telnet changes, and offering an interpretation of the Reverse Break control code. The author defends Hide-your-input as a way to simulate terminals that can suppress printing.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 393 argues that Telnet should preserve ways to hide typed input and support non-ASCII codes. It also proposes using a server-to-user Break signal to mark the end of a message on certain terminals.

subtitle: Comments on Telnet input hiding, data types and Reverse Break

tldr.problem: The author objects to proposed Telnet changes and asks how terminals with different capabilities should handle input, character codes and message boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC discusses Hide-your-input, alternate character codes and interpreting server-to-user Break as an end-of-message signal.
tldr.outcome: It offers design arguments and a proposed use for Reverse Break, rather than reporting a final protocol decision.

today: RFC 393 is a comment on Telnet protocol changes. It presents arguments and a proposed Reverse Break interpretation, not a record of the final decision.

sections.title: Functions Should Not Require Every Terminal
sections.content:
Joel Winett registers objections to two proposed Telnet changes and suggests an interpretation for Reverse Break. He argues that the protocol should not limit users just because some terminals cannot provide a particular function.

The RFC frames its comments around matching the capabilities available to a network user with those available to a local user of a time-sharing system.
sections.plainLanguage: The author argues that a feature should remain available even if some terminals cannot use it. Telnet implementations could ignore or simulate a feature when their equipment lacks direct support.

sections.title: Hide-your-input and Echo
sections.content: Hide-your-input lets a virtual terminal simulate a terminal that can suppress printing. Winett describes it as a special case related to echo control: a server can handle input without showing the typed characters. He suggests adding a following byte to specify how many characters to conceal, while retaining No-echo for terminals that can suppress printing themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: Some users need typed characters hidden, for example when a terminal cannot suppress printing on its own. The author suggests a way to state how many characters should be concealed.

sections.title: Alternate Character Codes
sections.content: The RFC argues that Telnet should support character codes other than ASCII, including EBCDIC. An alternate code should define its Telnet control codes and provide a way to return to the network standard ASCII code when needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Some hosts use character codes other than ASCII. The author wants Telnet to define those codes and a way to switch back to ASCII.

sections.title: Reverse Break as an End-of-Message Signal
sections.content:
Winett proposes interpreting Break sent from a server to a user as an end-of-message marker. This could tell a line-at-a-time terminal when to display received characters even if they do not end in CR-LF. On a half-duplex terminal, it could also signal that input should stop so output can be displayed.

The author describes this as a proposed use for a direction that had not previously been defined.
sections.plainLanguage: A terminal may need a clear signal that a server has finished a message. The author proposes using Reverse Break for that signal, especially when a terminal cannot display input and output at once.
